name: Act of March 2, 1889: the Standing Rock reservation (Royce 702)
citation: Act of March 2, 1889, ch. 405, 25 Stat. 888 (in force by proclamation of February 10, 1890)
nations: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe (Hunkpapa and Sihasapa Lakota, Yanktonai Dakota)
promises: The Act set apart for the Indians receiving rations at the Standing Rock agency the lands between the Cannon Ball River, the Missouri, a line ten miles north of the Moreau, and the 102nd meridian (Royce).

The Act of March 2, 1889 divided the Great Sioux Reservation into separate reservations; section 21 opened the rest to sale for the benefit of the Sioux, and section 19 kept in force all provisions of the 1868 treaty and the 1877 agreement not in conflict with it (Court of Claims, 105 Ct. Cl. 725).

breaches.what: The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe says Congress reduced the Great Sioux Reservation by the 1889 Act and opened it to non-Indian settlement, leaving Standing Rock checkerboarded, and holds its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights fully in force.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, History page (Wayback Machine copy of June 15, 2021)

today: In 1946 the Court of Claims held that the United States illegally charged food rations it owed the Sioux under the 1877 agreement, and certain agency costs, against Standing Rock trust funds (case C-531 (24)); those funds came from land sales under later Acts (1895 to 1910). It allowed $762,430.25 but set the recoveries off against reimbursable expenditures under section 17 of the 1889 Act and dismissed all seven petitions, so nothing was paid (105 Ct. Cl. 725). The Supreme Court vacated that judgment and remanded the cases on December 16, 1946 to consider the Indian Claims Commission Act; the Court of Claims re-entered it unchanged on June 28, 1948 (112 Ct. Cl. 50), and certiorari was denied in 1949 (as cited in ICC Docket 119, 34 Ind. Cl. Comm. 230). That ruling concerns the 1877 ration duty and the later sale funds, not this reservation's land under the 1889 Act, so it is not counted as a breach of this record.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the 1889 Act divided the Great Sioux Reservation and opened its land to non-Indian settlement, leaving Standing Rock checkerboarded, and that its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights remain binding.

openQuestions: Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): removed the court-ruling breach on 105 Ct. Cl. 725 and moved it to today. The opinion grounds the illegal charges in article 5 of the 1877 agreement (19 Stat. 254) and the trust funds of the 1895 to 1910 sale Acts; the 1889 Act appears only through section 19 and as the source of the offsets. The 1946 judgment was vacated and re-entered unchanged in 1948 (112 Ct. Cl. 50). Status lowered to contested.

The 1889 Act itself and the land ceded under it are recorded under cession-1889-03-02-sioux (Royce 631 and 699). This Royce row is the reservation kept. It is not marked sameEventAs that record because this row is the land kept, not the land ceded.
Later reductions of this reservation by Acts of Congress after 1889 are not in Royce's schedule and are not researched here.
The ICC accounting dockets for each reservation (114 to 119) were seen in the index but not read for this record.
The Standing Rock history page was read through the archived copy cited by cession-1889-03-02-sioux, not reloaded in this pass.

plain.promised: The 1889 Act gave the Standing Rock people their own reservation out of the Great Sioux Reservation.
plain.happened: The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe says the Act broke up its land and opened it to non-Indian settlement. No court or claims commission finding about this reservation under the 1889 Act was found.
plain.today: A 1946 Court of Claims ruling on rations paid from Standing Rock trust funds concerns the 1877 agreement and later land sales; nothing was paid on it.
